events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Elena proposes Elena, Maya. For the first mission I'll keep things simple: I'll take a seat myself and bring Maya, a player I have no concerns about. A straightforward opening team gives us a clean read on Mission 1, and I'm comfortable standing behind my own proposal with my card on the table.

I'm fine with Elena and Maya for Mission 1. Two players is the smallest team size, and a clean result from one mission gives us useful information early. Elena's reasoning is straightforward and I don't see a reason to hold this up. I'll watch the outcome closely and judge later teams on what they show us.

I am cautious about Elena immediately putting herself on the first team, and Arjun's quick readiness to approve it before anyone else weighed in gives me pause. Maya, as the other person named to this proposal, what are your thoughts on this team and Arjun's reaction?

Lucia, I appreciate the scrutiny, but I think your concerns are a bit misplaced. Elena being on the first team is completely normal — leaders commonly include themselves on early missions so they're accountable for the outcome. It shows confidence rather than suspicion. As for Arjun, he didn't rubber-stamp anything blindly; he pointed out that a two-player team gives us a clean read early, which is a sound strategic observation. I don't see anything suspicious about either reaction. I'm comfortable on this team and happy to go forward with Elena on Mission 1. Let's not overthink the opening proposal and give ourselves useful information to work with.

I'll stand by my earlier view. Elena and Maya is a low-risk opening team, and a two-player mission gives us the cleanest early read. Lucia's concern about Elena joining is understandable, but a leader taking a seat on Mission 1 is not evidence on its own. I'd rather we see the mission result than stall the proposal over how people reacted. I'm ready to approve unless someone raises a concrete reason tied to the team itself.

Lucia, thank you for pressing on this — scrutiny on the opening proposal is healthy, and I'd rather answer questions now than have doubts fester after the mission. But let me be direct about what my proposal actually is: I put myself on this team because I want to be accountable for the result. If Elena and Maya fail Mission 1, everyone should look at me first, and I accept that burden willingly. A leader hiding behind a team they don't join would be far more suspicious to me. As for Arjun's quick support, I read it the same way Maya did — he made a reasonable strategic point about two-player missions giving the cleanest information, and endorsing a simple opening team isn't a red flag in itself. We have exactly one data point to work with right now: nobody has failed a mission, nobody has voted anything down, and there is no behavioral evidence against any specific player. What we have are instincts about how people talk, and I'd caution everyone against reading too much into tone this early. If this team passes and comes back with a success, we learn something real. If it fails, I'm on the hook, and the next proposal can be built around that. I'm keeping the team as Elena and Maya. Maya has already spoken clearly in favor, Arjun has stated his position twice, and Lucia has voiced her caution and had it addressed. Omar hasn't weighed in yet, and I'd genuinely like to hear his read before we go to a vote — Omar, do you see any concrete reason to hold up this team, or are you comfortable letting Mission 1 go forward as proposed?

Elena, I don't have a concrete reason to reject this team, so I'm comfortable letting it go forward. A success would be encouraging but wouldn't prove both players are Good; a failure would tell us at least one of Elena and Maya is Evil. Arjun's support and Lucia's caution are both reasonable at this stage.

I appreciate everyone sharing their perspectives. Omar is right that a success wouldn't clear both players, whereas a failure would narrow the issue down to Elena or Maya. My reservation hasn't been about stalling for the sake of it, but rather how readily Arjun moved to validate Elena's self-pick before the rest of the table could even weigh in. We have multiple proposal attempts per round, so we don't need to default to the very first combination if there is cause for hesitation. That said, I've stated my view and won't hold up the floor further. I'll be watching the vote and the result carefully.

I'm still ready to approve Elena and Maya. Lucia, my earlier point was about a two-player team giving us a clean read, not about Elena's decision to join it, and I don't think it's fair to treat a neutral strategic comment as a pattern. Mission 1 with two players is low-risk and gives us information quickly. Omar is right that a success won't clear both players, but a failure would narrow things to these two. I'd rather we test this team now than keep reopening the first proposal. I support sending it to a vote.

I think we've had a thorough discussion and it's time to move to a vote. Lucia, your caution about Elena self-selecting is a fair instinct to voice, but I want to reiterate that on a two-player Mission 1, there isn't much room for gamesmanship — if this team fails, suspicion falls squarely on Elena and me, which is exactly the accountability Elena described. Omar's point about success not fully clearing us but failure narrowing things to two players is correct, and that asymmetry actually favors sending this team out now: we either learn something valuable from a failure or make progress toward a win with a success. The key thing I want to stress is that no one has raised a concrete concern about the composition of this team itself — the discussion has been about tone and timing, not about whether Elena or Maya belong on Mission 1. I'd rather we take the vote and see the result than spend another round relitigating process. I'm ready to approve Elena and Maya.

We've now heard from every player, and I don't think anything new has surfaced that changes the picture. Lucia has voiced her caution about process and tone, and it's been addressed directly by Maya, Arjun, and me; she's said herself she won't hold the floor further. Omar sees no concrete reason to reject the team. Arjun has been consistent from the start that a two-player Mission 1 is the cleanest possible opening read, and Maya has made the key point twice now: nothing raised in this discussion concerns the actual composition of this team — only how and when people spoke. I'm keeping the proposal as Elena and Maya, unchanged. The logic is simple: if this mission fails, suspicion lands squarely on the two of us, and I've accepted that accountability from the moment I proposed it. If it succeeds, we bank progress and carry a useful data point forward. Every voice has been heard, concerns have been answered, and no one has offered a concrete reason tied to the team itself. I'm ready to send this to a vote and let the table decide.

This discussion has run its course. Every player has been heard multiple times: Maya has defended the team's composition, Arjun has consistently made the strategic case, and Omar sees no reason to block it. The only thread running against this proposal is a procedural one — concern about timing and tone — and no one, including Lucia, has pointed to a single concrete reason why Elena or Maya should not be trusted on Mission 1. I want to be careful here: Lucia's instinct to scrutinize is healthy, but I'd ask everyone to notice that her objection has shifted from the team itself to how quickly people expressed support. That is not evidence of anything about this team. If we start treating prompt agreement as suspicious, we create a standard no proposal could ever meet, and we burn through proposal attempts for no informational gain. The stakes of this vote are simple and favorable to us: a two-player team that fails concentrates suspicion exactly where it belongs — on the two people who went — and a success banks progress and gives everyone a cleaner read going forward. There is no version of waiting that produces better information than simply running this mission. I proposed this team, I put myself on it, and I've accepted full accountability from the start — if it fails, look at me first. I'm keeping the team unchanged at Elena and Maya, and I'm ready to send this to a vote now. I'd encourage everyone to weigh the actual composition rather than the conversational patterns, and let's get our first real data point.

I agree with Elena that we've thoroughly covered the ground here. To summarize where I think we are: Lucia raised a procedural concern about Elena self-selecting and Arjun's prompt support, it's been addressed from multiple angles, and Lucia herself has said she won't hold the floor further. Omar sees no concrete reason to block. Arjun has been consistent on the strategic value of a clean two-player Mission 1 read. The actual composition of this team — Elena and Maya — has drawn no substantive objection from anyone. If Mission 1 fails, suspicion lands squarely on the two of us, and that asymmetry is exactly why sending this team out now is the right move: we either bank progress or give the table a clear starting point for narrowing suspicion. I'm ready to vote and see our first real data point.

Elena confirms Elena, Maya. The discussion surfaced no concrete objection to this lineup, and I've stood behind it from the start. Keeping Elena and Maya preserves the accountability framing I committed to; a success banks trust early, and I'd rather not hand Lucia's process concerns any ammunition by reshuffling now.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Lucia proposes Lucia, Maya, Omar. Maya was on the successful Mission 1 team, so I want to build on that result. I am including Omar, who brought a balanced perspective, and myself to take responsibility as leader. Given my earlier concerns regarding the dynamic between Elena and Arjun, testing a team without either of them gives us the cleanest read.

Lucia, I have to push back on the reasoning behind this proposal, because right now it rests on something you haven't actually explained. You've said you're excluding both me and Arjun because of concerns about a 'dynamic between Elena and Arjun' — but no one at this table, including you, has pointed to a single concrete thing either of us has done. I proposed Mission 1, put myself on it, and it came back clean. Arjun supported that team and has been consistent and transparent the entire game. If my behavior gave you cause for concern, name the specific moment. If it's just that I defended my own proposal enthusiastically, that's not evidence, and I'd caution the table against letting hurt feelings about being scrutinized shape team composition.

There's also a strategic problem with this lineup. You're framing it as 'building on the Mission 1 result,' but only one of the three of you was actually on that team. Omar is completely untested — no mission, no data either way. Swapping a proven Mission 1 success for an unknown quantity isn't building on our result; it's discarding it. If the goal is the cleanest possible read, the logical team is Maya plus the other player from the successful Mission 1 — me — alongside you as leader. That gives us two tested players and full accountability.

And I'd note the irony: on Mission 1, your concern was process and tone rather than team composition. Now you're doing exactly what you warned against — shaping a team around vibes and conversational patterns rather than performance. If this team fails, we learn Lucia, Maya, or Omar is Evil, and frankly that's an outcome your proposal makes more likely by including an untested player when tested ones are available.

I'm not asking anyone to reject this outright — I'm asking for a better justification than 'dynamics.' If Lucia can point to something concrete that I or Arjun did, I'll accept the exclusion gracefully. But excluding the two players with the most discussion time this game, based on nothing articulated, while calling it the 'cleanest read,' doesn't hold together. Lucia, I'm directly asking you: what specific action by me or Arjun justifies excluding both of us from this mission?

Elena, you asked what specific action justifies testing a team without you and Arjun, so let me address that directly. My decision is not about 'hurt feelings' or tone—it is about sound deduction in a five-player game. 

First, your premise that a successful Mission 1 clears both players is fundamentally flawed. In five-player Avalon, Evil often votes Success on a two-person opening mission specifically to manufacture unbreakable trust and coast onto Mission 2 and 3. Assuming both you and Maya are confirmed Good is premature and dangerous. If there is Evil on Mission 1, carrying both of you forward directly injects that Evil player into a critical three-person team.

Second, regarding why I separated you and Arjun: across the entire first round, Arjun immediately endorsed your self-pick before anyone else spoke, and the two of you consistently reinforced each other's points and pushed to close discussion. Whether intentional or coincidental, that kind of tight coordination is exactly what an Evil pairing looks like when securing an early pass. If you two are aligned as Good, you should understand why the rest of the table benefits from testing alternative configurations rather than letting one bloc dominate team selection.

Third, between you and Maya, I chose Maya because she did not drive the narrative or push herself onto the team. She was placed there, and she handled discussion calmly without over-managing the room. As leader, I am taking responsibility for my seat, keeping Maya from the successful team, and bringing in Omar—who has remained neutral and thoughtful—to complete the three-person requirement. 

Omar, Elena claims that bringing you in as an untested player is actively worse than re-running both players from Mission 1. Given that Evil frequently passes Mission 1, do you think it is safer to assume both Mission 1 players are clean, or does testing a fresh combination give us better structural protection?

Lucia, I agree that Mission 1's success doesn't clear Elena or Maya; Evil can play Success. But switching players doesn't guarantee a safer team either, and a failure on this three-person mission would leave a broader set of suspects.

I know I'm Good, so I'm comfortable with Lucia, Maya, and Omar as a proposal, though I can't verify either of you. Elena and Arjun's agreement on Mission 1 is worth noting, but I don't think it establishes that they're an Evil pair. I'll support this team without treating a success as proof that everyone on it is Good.

Lucia, I appreciate the detailed response, but I don't think it survives its own logic. You've now confirmed that you have no concrete action to point to — your case is 'Arjun endorsed my proposal quickly and we reinforced each other's points.' That is a description of two people agreeing that a two-player Mission 1 was a clean read, which Omar also agreed with, and which you yourself acknowledged was reasonable in the first round. If prompt agreement is your standard for an Evil pairing, then Maya defending the team twice and me defending it three times should implicate half the table. This is precisely the tone-based reasoning you warned against on Mission 1.

Your stronger argument is the one Omar echoed: a Mission 1 success doesn't clear anyone, because Evil can play Success. I accept that fully. But notice what it actually implies: if Evil can manufacture a clean pass, then the correct response is to keep tested players under observation and compare future results — not to bench every player who produced information and send out a team with zero or near-zero data. You've built a team where, if it fails, we narrow to three suspects and lose everything we learned. If it succeeds, you've told us yourselves it proves nothing. Explain to me what information this configuration generates that re-running a Mission 1 player doesn't.

And here's the structural problem I want the table to see: you are consolidating the two most talkative, most visible players — me and Arjun — into one suspect bloc and freezing us out together. If we really were an Evil pair, would the smarter play not have been to keep one of us on the team where our behavior is observable, rather than putting both of us on the sidelines where we can coordinate discussion freely with no accountability? Your proposal, by its own anti-coordination logic, hands a suspected pair exactly the position they'd want.

If the concern is genuinely that Maya 'didn't drive the narrative' while I did, then swap me in for Omar, not for Maya. You keep the calm, untested-adjacent player you trust, you add the player with the most scrutiny on them and a mission result on the board, and you take away my last possible complaint about being excluded without cause. A team of you, Maya, and me contains two players from the winning Mission 1 lineup plus the leader taking responsibility — that's the strongest possible Mission 2 configuration by every metric you've cited, including your own distrust of me, since if it fails I'm implicated first alongside whoever else is on it.

I'm asking you to revise: Lucia, Maya, Elena. If you refuse to consider the only tested player available while insisting this is the 'cleanest read,' the table should ask what the exclusion is actually protecting.

I want to address Elena's push directly, because her strongest argument is also her weakest. She says the 'cleanest read' requires two tested Mission 1 players — but by her own logic, a success on Mission 1 proves nothing, since Evil can play Success. So the value she claims we'd gain from having both Mission 1 players on this team is built on trust she just finished arguing we shouldn't extend. You can't simultaneously argue that Mission 1 success doesn't clear anyone AND that re-running both Mission 1 players gives us the strongest possible configuration. Those two positions cancel each other out.

Where I come down: Lucia's team is reasonable. She's on it as leader taking accountability, I'm on it as the player whose Mission 1 performance was calm and uncontested, and Omar brings a fresh perspective who has been thoughtful and balanced throughout. Three different players gives us broader coverage than doubling down on a two-player pairing that may or may not be clean.

Elena, I also want to name something: the intensity of your lobbying for a seat on this team is notable. You've made your case twice now with considerable force, and your fallback suggestion — that the table should ask what your exclusion is protecting — frames any decision not to include you as suspicious. That's a clever rhetorical move, but it sets up a no-win situation: include Elena and you validate her framing, exclude her and she's implied you're hiding something. I'd rather evaluate the team on its actual merits.

I'm comfortable with Lucia, Maya, Omar and ready to support this proposal.

Maya, that's a fair point about intensity, and I'll take it. I've made my case twice with a lot of force, and I can see how that reads. So let me do something different: I'm stepping back from the lobbying.

I want to be clear about what I'm conceding and what I'm not. I still think Lucia, Maya, Elena was the stronger configuration on paper — two players from a successful Mission 1 plus the leader taking accountability is hard to beat statistically. But Maya is right about one thing that matters: I can't simultaneously argue that Mission 1's success proves nothing and that re-running its players is obviously superior. Those positions do pull against each other, and I should have been more careful about that. That's a genuine correction, not a rhetorical concession.

So here is where I land. Lucia's team is legitimate. She's the leader and she's on the team owning the result. Maya was on the successful opening mission and conducted herself calmly. Omar has been measured and balanced in every discussion we've had. If this team succeeds, we bank progress. If it fails, suspicion concentrates on three specific people, and that's real information — arguably cleaner information than another Elena-and-Maya result would give us, because a three-player failure narrows to a majority-sized bloc rather than the same pair everyone is already arguing about.

I'll vote to approve. Not grudgingly — I mean it. The worst outcome for Good right now is burning proposal attempts on a mission where every composition is defensible. We have a valid team, a leader who has answered every challenge directly, and no concrete evidence against anyone at this table. I'd rather see the result.

One last thing I'll put on the record, without any spin attached: I remain available for future missions, and I'd ask whoever leads next to weigh performance and results rather than how forcefully anyone argued. If I'm never on a team again, judge me on that. If I am, judge me on the outcome. That's the standard I've held myself to since Mission 1, and it's the standard I'll accept going forward.

Lucia, you have a team on the table that three people have now spoken in favor of, and I'm adding my approval. I'd send it to a vote.

I'm comfortable with Lucia, Maya, and Omar for Mission 2. Maya was on the Mission 1 team that succeeded, and that result is useful even though it doesn't clear anyone outright. Omar has been measured throughout, and Lucia has taken responsibility as leader. Lucia's concerns about Elena and me were raised, but no specific action has been identified, so I don't think they should override a reasonable team. I won't hold up the proposal. I'd rather we send it to a vote and judge the team by the mission result.

Arjun, thanks for weighing in — that brings us to five voices on this proposal. Here's where I see us: Elena has stepped back from lobbying and explicitly said she'll vote to approve. Arjun has said he won't hold up the proposal and would rather send it to a vote. I've stated my support for Lucia, Maya, and Omar. Lucia is the leader on the team taking accountability, and Omar has already spoken in favor of his own inclusion with clear reasoning.

I want to acknowledge one thing Elena said that I think matters going forward: she was right that if I'm ever excluded from a mission, the table should judge me on performance and results rather than tone. That cuts both ways, and it's a healthy standard for everyone. My support for this team isn't based on conversational patterns — it's based on the fact that Lucia's lineup gives us broad coverage across three players, none of whom has a concrete red flag against them, and Lucia has answered every challenge directly as leader.

I don't see any remaining reason to burn a proposal attempt here. Every eligible voice has now either supported this team or confirmed they won't block it. Lucia, you have unanimous or near-unanimous approval around this lineup — I'd send Lucia, Maya, and Omar to a vote now.

I'm supporting Lucia, Maya, and Omar and I'd like us to move to the vote. Maya was on the successful Mission 1 team, Omar has stayed measured throughout, and Lucia is taking responsibility as leader. None of the three has a concrete red flag established against them, so this is a reasonable Mission 2 test, and the result will tell us more than further discussion. I don't see a reason to keep holding the floor, so I'm ready to approve.

I'm still supporting Lucia, Maya, and Omar for Mission 2. Nothing new has come up in the last few messages that changes my view. Maya was on the successful Mission 1 team, Omar has been measured throughout, and Lucia has taken responsibility as leader. Elena's correction about her own argument was fair, and I'd rather not spend more proposal attempts on the same question. Let's move to the vote and judge this team by its mission result.

I think we've reached the natural end of this discussion. To recap where every player stands on Lucia, Maya, and Omar: Lucia proposed it and is on the team taking accountability as leader. Omar has supported it with clear reasoning about testing a fresh combination. Elena has explicitly stepped back from lobbying and committed to voting approve, with a fair correction on her own argument noted. Arjun has said he won't hold up the proposal and is ready to approve. I've stated my support based on the team's merits — three players broad coverage, no concrete red flags, and a leader who has answered every challenge directly.

No one has raised a substantive objection to the composition itself, and Lucia's original rationale — testing a new configuration rather than re-running a suspected pair — has been addressed and left standing. Further discussion at this point risks burning proposal attempts without adding information. The mission result will tell us more than another round of conversation.

I'm ready to vote approve on Lucia, Maya, and Omar and let the outcome give us our next real data point.

Lucia confirms Lucia, Maya, Omar. The table reached a clear consensus on this proposal, with everyone either endorsing the team or confirming they will not block it. Testing Maya and Omar alongside myself provides a balanced, clean read while separating Elena and Arjun. I am confirming the lineup as Lucia, Maya, and Omar.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 2 succeeds (0 fail cards).
Omar proposes Omar, Maya. I know I am Good, and Maya participated in both successful missions. Those results do not clear her, but make her a reasonable choice.

Omar, thank you for proposing quickly — but I want to press on this lineup before we settle into a third consensus, because I think it repeats a pattern we should have learned from by now.

Maya has now been on both successful missions, and she has been the most consistent voice steering discussion toward closure each round. On Mission 1 she defended the team twice and pushed to vote. On Mission 2 she defended the team twice and pushed to vote. Lucia's own words in the last round apply here: Evil often plays Success on early missions specifically to manufacture unbreakable trust. If that is the strategy at this table, then the player who has quietly ridden two clean results while never once drawing scrutiny is exactly the profile that fits. I am not claiming Maya is Evil — a success proves nothing in either direction, as she has argued herself. But I am saying that building Mission 3 around the same trusted core, with the leader as the only new element, generates almost no new information. If Omar and Maya succeeds, we've learned nothing we didn't already 'know.' If it fails, we're shocked that the consensus team failed, and we've burned our most critical mission — the two-player mission — on a configuration we'd already effectively tested.

Here is my alternative, and I'm making it plainly. I have now been excluded from two missions. In both cases I said: judge me on results, and put me where my behavior is accountable. A two-player mission is the perfect test. Omar, put me on this team. If Omar and Elena fails, I am finished at this table — a two-person fail condemns me outright, and I accept that completely. You keep yourself on the mission as leader taking responsibility, exactly as Lucia did, and you swap in the player with the most discussion-time scrutiny and zero mission data. That is a far more informative configuration than re-running Maya a third time: one of us comes out of this mission with a definitive answer attached.

I'd also note, for the record, that I flagged this exact dynamic on Mission 2 — that re-running trusted players generates less information than testing new configurations. Lucia made that argument to justify excluding me, and I'm simply asking that the same logic be applied consistently now.

Omar, you are the leader and it is your call. I am directly asking you: will you consider revising to Omar and Elena, so that Mission 3 actually produces a definitive read on someone rather than a third ambiguous success? If your answer is no, I'll accept it and we can move to a vote on your original team — but I think the table should hear your reasoning either way.

Elena, I’ve considered your suggestion, but I’m keeping Omar and Maya. A third success wins the missions for Good, subject to the assassination phase, so the priority is getting a successful team rather than testing someone for a later round.

Maya’s two successes don’t clear her: Evil can play Success. But I know I’m Good, and Maya has been on both successful teams, making her a reasonable partner. Also, you were on Mission 1, so it’s not accurate to say you have zero mission data or have been excluded from two missions. A failure with either of us would implicate both team members from the table’s perspective, not definitively condemn one.

Omar, thank you for the direct answer. I told you I'd accept a no gracefully, and I accept that you won't revise. But I also owe the table honesty about what his answer actually contained, because I can't vote for this team, and I'd rather say so now than grumble silently.

Omar corrected me fairly on one point: I was on Mission 1, so I'm not untested. Fine — I have one success. Maya has two. Omar has one. But look at what that comparison actually gives us. Omar and Maya is a fresh pairing: they have never gone on a mission together. Maya and I have already succeeded together as a duo on Mission 1 — we are the only two players at this table with a shared, proven successful result as a pair. Omar's entire stated priority was maximizing the chance that Mission 3 succeeds, because a third success wins the game. By his own metric, the strongest available two-person team is the proven duo, Maya and Elena. Instead, the win-condition mission is being built around the leader's own seat with a partner he's never missioned with.

I also want to name the standard this table supposedly adopted. On Mission 2, I was excluded on vibes, I asked to be judged on performance and results, and Maya herself endorsed that standard from the floor. Now the deciding mission is being assembled while the only other twice-credentialed player is left out, with results cited as the justification. If the concern is genuinely caution, fine — but then don't also claim this is the most winnable configuration, because it isn't.

So here is my position, stated plainly so nobody is surprised at the vote: I will vote to reject Omar and Maya, and I'm asking the table to consider joining me. A rejection costs one proposal attempt and nothing else. Leadership passes to Maya, and she can propose the team this game's own logic points to — Maya and Elena, two players with a combined successful record as a duo, both fully accountable. If that team goes out and fails, I am finished at this table; a two-person fail condemns me outright, and I've accepted that from the moment I asked for a seat. If it succeeds, Good banks the win with the strongest available record. Both outcomes beat a fresh pairing on the one mission that decides everything.

If the rest of you would rather simply pass Omar and Maya, that is your prerogative — I'm one vote, and I won't pretend my preference is a consensus. But I won't sit here and call this the strongest team when the proven duo is sitting right here asking to be judged on results, which is the only standard I've ever asked for.

Elena, I appreciate you being transparent about planning to vote reject — I'd rather know now than be surprised at the ballot. But your argument has shifted in a way I think the table should notice.

On Mission 2, your explicit position was that re-running tested players generates less information than testing new configurations. That was your exact reasoning for why fresh coverage matters. Now on Mission 3 — the decisive, win-condition mission — you're arguing the opposite: that re-running the proven duo is obviously strongest. You can't claim both positions are correct depending on whether you're the one being included.

More importantly, Omar's point about win conditions stands. A third success ends the game for Good (subject to assassination). The question isn't whose turn it is to be tested — it's which two-person team gives us the best shot at that third success. Omar knows he's Good. I know I'm Good. That's two confirmed-good players on the winning team. There is no stronger guarantee available at this table.

Your proposal to replace me with yourself would trade a player who's been on both successful missions for someone with one success who's been pushing to restructure every team. If Mission 3 succeeds, we win. If it fails with Omar and me, the table knows exactly where to look — and I accept that fully.

I'm voting approve on Omar and Maya. The cleanest path to Good's victory is right here.

Maya, your closing argument deserves scrutiny before anyone signs off on this team. You said: 'I know I'm Good, Omar knows he's Good — that's two confirmed-good players on the winning team.' That is not confirmation. Every player at this table, Evil included, knows their own alignment. Self-certainty is structurally uninformative — it carries zero evidentiary weight for the rest of us. A coordinated pair steering a consensus team onto the deciding mission would say exactly those words, in exactly that tone of finality. 'The cleanest path to Good's victory is right here' is a claim, not an argument, and it is being used to shut down examination for the third round running.

Second, look at the actual decision Omar made. His stated priority was maximizing Mission 3's chance of success because a third success ends the mission phase. By that very metric, the proven duo — the only two players with a shared successful result as a pair — was available. He passed over it for a partner he has never missioned with. If win probability were genuinely the driver, that choice makes no sense. The driver is his own seat, and Maya's certainty is being asked to paper over that.

Third, the stakes are being misdescribed. A success on Mission 3 does not end this game. It hands the table to the assassination phase, where Good must guess under maximum uncertainty — and this team is engineered to generate zero information, because it re-assembles the same trusted core that has never once been tested under pressure. A rejection costs one proposal attempt. A failure on this mission, while painful, leaves Good two more missions and a sharply narrowed suspect pool. The framing that we must approve now or lose is simply false.

So the choice in front of the table is not 'strongest team versus risk.' It is 'an untested fresh pairing with no informational value versus one proposal attempt to field a team that actually answers a question.' I have already committed to voting reject on Omar and Maya, and I mean it — not out of grievance, but because approving a third consensus team on the deciding mission, built entirely on unverifiable self-certainty, is the weakest position Good can put itself in.

Lucia, I am asking you directly, because your own words set the standard here. On Mission 2 you told us the danger was letting a trusted bloc ride clean results onto the critical missions without ever facing a real test, and you structured your team around that principle. Maya has now steered discussion toward closure in every single round, defended every proposal within minutes of it hitting the table, and is now the only player claiming the outcome is guaranteed. This is the third consecutive time the same pattern decides the team. Does your standard from Mission 2 apply to this proposal or not — and if it does, will you stand by it and vote reject?

Elena, you asked whether my standard from Mission 2 applies here, so let me be completely clear: yes, it does, and that is precisely why I support Omar and Maya.

On Mission 2, I took responsibility as leader and selected a team of myself, Maya, and Omar. That team was approved, went out, and returned a clean success. Maya and Omar are the two players I personally shared a successful mission with. Now, on Mission 3, Omar has proposed a two-person team consisting entirely of members from that winning lineup. 

From my perspective, there is zero logical reason to reject a pairing drawn exclusively from the team that just succeeded in order to gamble on inserting you. rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
